Paired frozen-score inference for conditional ratios

Source: vignettes/conditional-late-inference.Rmd
conditional-late-inference.Rmd

The supported affine_ratio_dnn() and clate_dnn() workflows average two signals using common DNN weights, then take their ratio. Exact weights and one neighbor per subsample are the defaults; asymptotic DNN and general k use the same paired calculation. The worked example below is exact. This article explains the paired covariance calculation and its numerical diagnostics. Start with Conditional LATE from supplied nuisance predictions for the economic target and input roles.

A four-observation calculation

The following fixed arrays isolate the computation from nuisance learning. The signed denominator signal is intentional.

fit <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = matrix(1:4, ncol = 1), x0 = 0,
  numerator = c(2, 1, 4, 3), denominator = c(1, -1, 2, 1), s = 2,
  return = c("W", "signals", "deletions", "pseudo_values")
)
fit$W
#>           [,1]
#> [1,] 0.5000000
#> [2,] 0.3333333
#> [3,] 0.1666667
#> [4,] 0.0000000
fit$components
#>      numerator denominator
#> [1,]         2         0.5
coef(fit)
#> target_1 
#>        4

The weights are (1/2,1/3,1/6,0)(1/2,1/3,1/6,0), the components are (2,1/2)(2,1/2), and the fitted ratio is four. Here s counts observations competing to be the nearest in each subsample. It does not count the nonzero weights.

For each deletion, keep the signals, target point, metric and order s fixed, and recompute exact weights on the retained observations. The fitted ratio remains fixed when forming the score. This calculation requires s < n and involves no nuisance refitting.

fit$deletions[, , 1]
#>          [,1]      [,2]
#> [1,] 2.000000 0.0000000
#> [2,] 2.666667 1.3333333
#> [3,] 1.666667 0.3333333
#> [4,] 1.666667 0.3333333
P <- fit$pseudo_values[, , 1]
P
#>              [,1] [,2]
#> [1,] 2.000000e+00    2
#> [2,] 4.440892e-16   -2
#> [3,] 3.000000e+00    1
#> [4,] 3.000000e+00    1
centered <- sweep(P, 2, colMeans(P), "-")
V <- crossprod(centered) / (4 * 3)
V
#>      [,1] [,2]
#> [1,]  0.5 0.50
#> [2,]  0.5 0.75
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(unname(V), matrix(c(.5, .5, .5, .75), 2))))

The pseudo-values are PY=(2,0,3,3)P_Y=(2,0,3,3) and PD=(2,−2,1,1)P_D=(2,-2,1,1). The first deleted denominator is zero, but all component deletion averages and pseudo-values are finite. A jackknife of deleted ratios would perform an undefined division at this deletion; it is a different statistic.

With θ̂=4\hat\theta=4, score pseudo-values are Qj=θ̂PD,j−PY,jQ_j=\hat\theta P_{D,j}-P_{Y,j}. Their centered variation gives the same variance as the paired component covariance:

V̂θ=VYY+θ̂2VDD−2θ̂VYDΔ̂D2. \widehat V_\theta= \frac{V_{YY}+\hat\theta^2V_{DD}-2\hat\theta V_{YD}} {\hat\Delta_D^2}. 

Q <- fit$theta * P[, 2] - P[, 1]
Q
#> [1]  6 -8  1  1
variance <- sum((Q - mean(Q))^2) / (4 * 3 * fit$components[1, 2]^2)
c(paired_variance = variance,
  omitting_cross_covariance = (V[1, 1] + fit$theta^2 * V[2, 2]) /
    fit$components[1, 2]^2)
#>           paired_variance.denominator omitting_cross_covariance.denominator 
#>                                    34                                    50
fit$theta_vcov
#> [[1]]
#>       theta
#> theta    34
fit$neff
#> [1] 2.571429
fit$theta_omega
#> [[1]]
#>          theta
#> theta 87.42857
stopifnot(abs(variance - 34) < 1e-10,
          abs(fit$neff - 18 / 7) < 1e-10,
          abs(fit$theta_omega[[1]][1, 1] - 612 / 7) < 1e-10)

Discarding the cross-covariance gives variance 50 instead of 34 in this example. Dividing the numerator standard error by the first stage also omits denominator uncertainty.

Keep the variance scales distinct

Returned field Meaning
components[, "numerator"] Reduced form for a CLATE fit
components[, "denominator"] First stage for a CLATE fit
component_vcov[[j]] Paired component covariance on the estimator scale
theta_vcov[[j]] Ratio variance on the estimator scale
theta_omega[[j]] neff[j] * theta_vcov[[j]], local-limit covariance estimate
se[j] Square root of the ratio variance
neff[j] Inverse sum of squared reporting weights

theta_vcov already includes the local sample-size scaling. Do not divide it by neff again. Covariance lists are marginal across reporting targets; they do not supply covariance between different targets or simultaneous confidence bands.

summary(fit)
#> Components: numerator = numerator; denominator = denominator
#> Ratio statuses: ok=1
#>          estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high
#> target_1        4     5.831     0.686  0.4927   -7.428     15.43
confint(fit)
#>           conf.low conf.high
#> target_1 -7.428456  15.42846
diagnostics(fit)
#> <dnn_diagnostics>
#>   targets: 1
#>   n_eff  : min=2.5714, median=2.5714, max=2.5714
#>   weights: max(top5 share)=1, max(weight)=0.5
#>   dist   : available for 1/1 target(s)

Effective sample size describes rank-weight concentration. It is not a count of compliers. Physical radius, instrument-arm support, score dispersion and first-stage strength can vary even when neff is the same. The largest centered pseudo-value-square shares attribute fitted variance to deletion indices, including rank changes; they differ from raw weighted score contributions.

Singular covariance and signed signals

With perfect compliance, treatment equals instrument assignment and the augmented first-stage signal equals one. Its estimated variance is zero, while the outcome signal and ratio can still have positive variance. Positive definiteness of the full two-component covariance is unnecessary for this scalar calculation.

A <- c(0, 1, 0, 1)
sig <- iv_augmented_signals(
  Y = c(0, 1, .2, 1.2), D = A, A = A, e = rep(.5, 4),
  m_y0 = rep(0, 4), m_y1 = rep(.5, 4),
  m_d0 = rep(0, 4), m_d1 = rep(1, 4)
)
constant_first_stage <- affine_ratio_dnn(
  X = matrix(1:4), x0 = 0, numerator = sig$phi_y,
  denominator = sig$phi_d, s = 2
)
sig$phi_d
#> [1] 1 1 1 1
constant_first_stage$component_vcov
#> [[1]]
#>             numerator denominator
#> numerator        0.18           0
#> denominator      0.00           0

Even in a one-sided compliance model, eligible nonparticipants can have negative augmented first-stage signals:

iv_augmented_signals(
  Y = c(0, 1), D = c(0, 1), A = c(1, 1), e = c(.5, .5),
  m_y0 = c(0, 0), m_y1 = c(1, 1), m_d1 = c(.6, .6), one_sided = TRUE
)$phi_d
#> [1] -0.6  1.4

The output is (−0.6,1.4)(-0.6,1.4). Treatment predictions may lie in [0,1][0,1], but augmented treatment signals need not. The estimator keeps signed signals and finite negative denominators. At an exactly zero aggregate denominator it retains both components and their covariance, while reporting an undefined ratio and unavailable Wald interval.

The near_zero_denominator flag is a numerical cancellation diagnostic; it does not change the estimator. The first-stage standardized magnitude is a different, descriptive diagnostic. No universal weak-instrument cutoff is attached to it. An exactly zero score norm gives a computational SE of zero and wald_available = FALSE, with NA interval bounds.

Which IV effect is being reported?

Within a reporting profile, consider two equally common adjustment strata:

strata <- data.frame(compliance = c(1 / 4, 3 / 4),
                     effect = c(0, 2), propensity = c(1 / 2, 1 / 4))
with(strata, c(
  CLATE = sum(compliance * effect) / sum(compliance),
  average_stratum_LATE = mean(effect),
  residualized_IV = sum(propensity * (1 - propensity) * compliance * effect) /
    sum(propensity * (1 - propensity) * compliance)
))
#>                CLATE average_stratum_LATE      residualized_IV 
#>             1.500000             1.000000             1.384615

The three answers are 3/23/2, 11, and 18/1318/13. Residualized IV introduces instrument-variance weights. Its target can coincide with CLATE under additional restrictions, but equality should be checked. The local IV-GMM article documents the package’s separate residualized moment and covariance workflow.

What justifies full-sample inference?

For response R=Y,DR=Y,D, holding candidate nuisance functions fixed gives the exact conditional mean error

(e−e0){mR,1−mR,1,0e+mR,0−mR,0,01−e}. (e-e_0)\left\{\frac{m_{R,1}-m_{R,1,0}}e+ \frac{m_{R,0}-m_{R,0,0}}{1-e}\right\}.

This product removes first-order nuisance mean bias. Individual scores still depend on observations used for training. The affine theorem also requires expected prediction convergence over the specified retained fits, quantitative deletion stability, bounded envelopes and exceptional-event control, together with oracle moments, local design, positive score variance, fixed relevance and point-target undersmoothing. Proof-only deleted nuisance fits are distinct from the frozen-array deletions used for standard errors.

The bounded clate_demo_data() construction and its designated growing ridge-series training rule provide a concrete sufficient route developed in the research notes. The internal ridge adapter is a reference study tool; clate_dnn() still accepts predictions rather than fitting learners. Array parity tests verify the algorithm. They do not prove asymptotic learner rates or causal assumptions. Practical forests, unbounded asset outcomes and data-selected geometry need their own justification.

Ratio confidence sets

The experimental ratio_confidence_set() helper inverts the candidate moment inequality

(Δ̂Y−θΔ̂D)2≤z2(VYY−2θVYD+θ2VDD). (\widehat\Delta_Y-\theta\widehat\Delta_D)^2 \le z^2(V_{YY}-2\theta V_{YD}+\theta^2V_{DD}).

This helper uses the same paired estimator-scale covariance. It can return bounded intervals, singletons, half-lines, two rays, all real numbers or empty sets. It remains separate from confint(), which reports pointwise Wald intervals for fitted ratio objects.

ratio_confidence_set(fit$components, fit$component_vcov)
#> Paired ratio confidence sets
#>   target 1: two_rays (-Inf, -0.60543] U [1.3053, Inf) (ok)
sets <- ratio_confidence_set(
  rbind(c(2, 1), c(3, 0), c(0, 0)),
  list(diag(c(.5, 0)), diag(2), matrix(0, 2, 2))
)
sets
#> Paired ratio confidence sets
#>   target 1: bounded [0.6141, 3.3859] (ok)
#>   target 2: two_rays (-Inf, -1.1588] U [1.1588, Inf) (ok)
#>   target 3: all_real (-Inf, Inf) (ok)
vapply(sets, function(x) x$type, character(1))
#> [1] "bounded"  "two_rays" "all_real"

Finite endpoints are included; infinite endpoints use open notation. An unresolved result has a numerical status and no asserted set geometry, and differs from a mathematically empty result. Materially indefinite covariance is rejected. Power-of-two scaling and stable roots limit overflow and cancellation; near-boundary or unrepresentable calculations remain explicit in the returned record.

With a deterministic nonzero denominator, the helper computes the interval width directly from the numerator SE. This preserves small positive uncertainty that can disappear when quadratic coefficients are expanded. An apparent repeated root of rounded coefficients alone cannot certify a singleton; an uncertifiable result is unresolved. If the estimator’s component covariance underflows despite nonzero component variation, it returns unavailable covariance with numerical_failure status. The helper rejects that unavailable input rather than interpreting it as zero variance.

At a fixed true candidate, inclusion probability is the acceptance probability of that one candidate’s score test. Simultaneous validity of all candidate tests is unnecessary for this pointwise statement. The test still needs its own local-score CLT, consistent variance, nuisance and bias conditions, including positive variance. Algebraic zero-variance branches are not automatically covered by that theorem. Uniform coverage over changing models with increasingly weak first stages requires an additional sequence-specific argument; the quadratic calculation does not establish it.
